scenes.tts: Why can a strawberry runner make a copy, while brothers and sisters are different? Watch one garden tell both stories. A runner stretches from one plant and roots nearby. It has one parent. This is asexual reproduction. The new plant usually carries the same genetic information.

scenes.visual: Hook first, no title yet. In a large schematic garden, one strawberry plant fills the left half. Its runner visibly grows across the soil and roots as a matching plant. A one-parent arrow follows the runner. Keep leaves swaying while the question stays large on the right.
scenes.narration: Why can a strawberry runner make a copy, while brothers and sisters are different? Watch one garden tell both stories. A runner stretches from one plant and roots nearby. It has one parent. This is asexual reproduction. The new plant usually carries the same genetic information.

scenes.visual: The garden remains visible and moving. Overlay the title 'Copies, Halves, and Pairs' for two seconds, then let it dissolve into the chromosome model.

scenes.tts: Sexual reproduction takes another path. Two sex cells join, usually one from each of two parents. In animals, those cells are sperm and egg. Before they join, a problem must be solved. Body cells carry chromosomes in pairs. Joining two fully paired cells would double the chromosome number.

scenes.visual: Transform the two rooted plants into two large schematic parent cells. Each contains two chromosome pairs made from one blue and one gold bar. Move the cells toward a central join point, then stop them as a doubled chromosome count appears above the join point with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Sexual reproduction takes another path. Two sex cells join, usually one from each of two parents. In animals, those cells are sperm and egg. Before they join, a problem must be solved. Body cells carry chromosomes in pairs. Joining two fully paired cells would double the chromosome number.

scenes.tts: Follow the blue and gold bars. Each color marks one member of a chromosome pair. The pair carries the same kinds of genes in the same general places. One member came from the mother, and one from the father. A body cell keeps both members together.

scenes.visual: Zoom into one large schematic body cell. Blue and gold bars stay paired by length: one long pair and one short pair. Matching gene-position tick marks glow at the same places on each pair. On-screen only, show 'body cell: 46' and '23 pairs' in a small human example panel.
scenes.narration: Follow the blue and gold bars. Each colour marks one member of a chromosome pair. The pair carries the same kinds of genes in the same general places. One member came from the mother, and one from the father. A body cell keeps both members together.

scenes.tts: Which move could let two sex cells join without doubling the chromosome number? Watch the bars. Should every pair stay together, or should each cell carry only half? Make your prediction.
scenes.caption: Which move could let two sex cells join without doubling the chromosome number? Watch the bars. Should every pair stay together, or should each cell carry only half? Make your prediction.
scenes.visual: Hold the large cell in the center. Above it, animate two possible arrows: paired bars staying together, or blue and gold members separating. End with both choices neutral and a large question mark.
scenes.narration: Which move could let two sex cells join without doubling the chromosome number? Watch the bars. Should every pair stay together, or should each cell carry only half? Make your prediction.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the question on screen. The two choice arrows pulse slowly, but reveal no answer.

scenes.tts: Meiosis solves the problem. The members of each pair separate. A sex cell receives one chromosome from every pair. Its chromosome number is half the body-cell number. Here is the rule. Sexual reproduction: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.
scenes.caption: Meiosis solves the problem. The members of each pair separate. A sex cell receives one chromosome from every pair. Its chromosome number is half the body-cell number. Here is the rule. Sexual reproduction: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.
scenes.visual: Reveal the separating choice. Blue and gold bars glide along curved paths into green sex cells, each receiving one long and one short bar. A counter visibly changes from '46' in the schematic body-cell example to '23' in each sex cell. The one-rule line appears only as the movement finishes.
scenes.narration: Meiosis solves the problem. The members of each pair separate. A sex cell receives one chromosome from every pair. Its chromosome number is half the body-cell number. Here is the rule. Sexual reproduction: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.

scenes.tts: Now a sperm and egg move together. Fertilization joins them into one new cell. Their half sets make full pairs again. Each restored pair has one chromosome from each parent. The chromosome number returns to the usual body-cell number instead of growing with every generation.
scenes.caption: Now a sperm and egg move together. Fertilization joins them into one new cell. Their half sets make full pairs again. Each restored pair has one chromosome from each parent. The chromosome number returns to the usual body-cell number instead of growing with every generation.
scenes.visual: Carry two green sex cells from opposite sides into the center. Their bars slide together by length inside one white fertilized cell. On-screen only, animate '23 + 23 = 46'. Keep every bar moving into its partner before the completed pairs settle.
scenes.narration: Now a sperm and egg move together. Fertilization joins them into one new cell. Their half sets make full pairs again. Each restored pair has one chromosome from each parent. The chromosome number returns to the usual body-cell number instead of growing with every generation.

scenes.tts: Look again at the bar count. Halving does not mean cutting chromosomes into pieces. It means placing one whole chromosome from every pair into a sex cell. When the cells join, the partners form pairs again. This movement can repeat across generations without a steady rise in chromosome number.

scenes.visual: Keep one blue-and-gold pair large at center. Briefly show scissors beside a chromosome, then move them away under a clear 'not cut' label. Slide each whole bar into a separate green cell, then bring two whole bars back together as a pair in a white cell.

scenes.tts: The picture used animal sperm and egg cells. Plants take an extra step. Meiosis first makes spores, and sex cells form later. Those sex cells still carry half. The simple model also has an exception: rare DNA changes can make an asexual copy imperfect.

scenes.visual: Keep the completed paired cell at center. At left, a small schematic flower transforms a parent cell into spores, then into green sex cells. At right, return to the runner plant and add one tiny changed leaf spot labelled 'rare DNA change', without making it look typical.

scenes.tts: Return to the garden. The runner grows from one parent, so it usually carries that parent's genetic information. Sexual offspring begin when half sets join. Meiosis prevents chromosome number from doubling. Fertilization restores the pairs. The next question is why those half sets are not all alike.

Let different blue-and-gold bar arrangements drift faintly behind the paired cell as an unanswered visual question, with no claim that any mix is guaranteed.
